items.title: SCMP: "Beijing should expand central government borrowing and accelerate local debt restructuring, as China’s relatively low price levels offer a rar...
items.description_html:
SCMP: "Beijing should expand central government borrowing and accelerate local debt restructuring, as China’s relatively low price levels offer a rare window for stronger fiscal support to bolster demand, according to some prominent Chinese economists."

As always, this is pretty confused. It makes sense for businesses and households to borrow when interest rates are low because lower financing costs can raise net returns. Governments are different.

Government borrowing is largely a transfer from one sector of the economy to another. In China’s case, “cheap” borrowing reduces the returns to net lenders, mainly households, in order to subsidize net borrowers.

Yet Beijing knows that sustaining long-term growth requires doing the opposite: increasing the household share of GDP. The problem is that this has proved extraordinarily difficult, and the confusion over borrowing costs helps explain why.

Lower interest rates are not necessarily good for China. They can actually deepen the imbalance by reducing the income of net savers, largely households, while making it cheaper for borrowers to sustain additional investment, much of which is already generating diminishing returns.

Beijing should therefore not be looking for clever ways to tax households so that it can borrow more cheaply. It should be looking for ways to raise household income and discourage further misallocation of capital.
https://sc.mp/yupro?utm_source=twitter&utm_campaign=3368259&utm_medium=share_widget via @scmpnews

items.title: Li Xunlei, Chief Economist at Zhongtai Financial: “The conclusion is clear: the places that built the most expressways were often those where freight...
items.description_html:
Li Xunlei, Chief Economist at Zhongtai Financial: “The conclusion is clear: the places that built the most expressways were often those where freight demand grew the least.”

The East is Red has translated an article by Li Xunlei on how China’s infrastructure spending may have served the economy poorly, something he seems to have been worrying about even longer than I have.

He attributes local officials’ enthusiasm for infrastructure partly to the belief that “if you want to get rich, build roads first,” and partly to the tendency to measure performance by highly visible projects rather than underlying problems such as population outflows and weak local industries.

The underlying mistake is common, and not just in China. Policymakers too often treat infrastructure spending as a source of growth, so that when an economy faces institutional, demographic or other constraints that keep growth below expectations, their response is to increase infrastructure spending in order to goose economic activity.

But this often has it backwards. If those constraints limit productivity growth, the value of additional infrastructure is likely to be lower, not higher. Infrastructure spending, in other words, is not a source of growth. It is a cost of growth, and it makes an economy richer only when the productivity gains it generates exceed the cost of building and maintaining it.

Otherwise it makes the economy poorer. And the fact that local-government debt has grown so much faster than provincial GDP for nearly two decades suggests how years of overinvestment can leave less productive regions deeply indebted, with spectacular infrastructure but inadequate economic activity to support it.

It is encouraging that more and more Chinese economists and policy advisers are questioning this model. But changing it will be difficult. Infrastructure projects reliably produce a short-term boost to activity, making them especially tempting when growth slows and unemployment rises, until debt constraints finally make further spending impossible.
https://www.eastisread.com/p/li-xunlei-on-chinas-transport-overcapacity

items.title: RT menaka doshi: India has committed over 4.5 trillion rupees ($47 billion) to building a manufacturing economy. And that’s just what the federal gov...
items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
India has committed over 4.5 trillion rupees ($47 billion) to building a manufacturing economy. And that’s just what the federal government has allocated to its production-linked incentive scheme across 14 sectors (1.91 trillion rupees), semiconductor missions (1.93 trillion rupees) and the new mobile-phone manufacturing scheme (625 billion rupees). States offer incentives of their own, making that a considerably larger number.

Sure, this has boosted investment and jobs. Also, smartphones, led by iPhones, are now a top export item from India.

But the share of manufacturing in GDP has stagnated for a decade and the country is still viewed more as an assembler of products than a deeply integrated manufacturer.

How long will that transition take, and when will Indian manufacturers stop needing taxpayer support?

In an interview, Sunil Vachani, chairman of Dixon Technologies India Limited, a leading electronics manufacturing services company, talks to me about

Smartphone sales slowdown
Scope for diversification
Reliance on subsidies and incentives
From assembly to value-added manufacturing
Investments from China
Becoming innovators
Boosting profit margins

Sunil offered a detailed view of India's manufacturing economy.

Read a quick take here 👇
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-23/india-s-over-50-billion-manufacturing-bet-to-pay-off-by-2030-dixon-says?srnd=undefined

items.title: The macros have played out reasonably okay. The challenges are coming on account of gold rate volatility. When that happens many customers tend to be ...
items.description_html:
The macros have played out reasonably okay. The challenges are coming on account of gold rate volatility. When that happens many customers tend to be on the fence, Titan MD Ajoy Chawla said to me.

In Q1 FY27, Titan's management had described the operating conditions as being not so favorable. I asked Chawla if Q2 had been better.

"There's one school of thought which says gold price is going to keep going up. Another school of thought says gold price will get corrected down because government may reduce customs duty. And why are they saying that? Because there's been a lot of smuggling of gold which has gone up in the country.

The government had to raise the duties because they needed to manage the balance-of-payment related pieces. But they are mindful of the fact that this is not sustainable. So at some stage they may need to bring it down now. As to when, the customers will keep guessing.

And there is no very sharp reason in Q2 to buy gold. The big purchases for jewelry happens in Q3 and Q4 for the festivals, weddings and festivals. So a lot of people tend to sit on the fence and see what to do.

I might be wrong, but I am just making a prediction that if duty comes down you will find a gold rush."

items.title: RT Citrini: There’s no way any of us can predict the impact that AI will have on companies, sectors or consumer behavior (which has been, for all of ...
items.description_html:
RT Citrini
There’s no way any of us can predict the impact that AI will have on companies, sectors or consumer behavior (which has been, for all of history until now, human behavior).

But to claim that it won’t have an impact and simply brush it off lacks both humility and creativity.

Tactics that worked when consumer behavior was dictated by human psychology will fall by the wayside, and those that fail to adapt will be left behind.

Every day from now on we will see new examples of areas where friction was profitable becoming cost centers for companies that don’t react in a timely enough manner.

Today you might realize just how many flight credits, loyalty points or promotional offers you’ve never used that will end up utilized by agents. What impact will that have?

Tomorrow, you might see something that makes you ask how much money health insurers make simply because people won’t sit on the phone for 5 hours trying to get coverage approved unless it’s a massive expense and/or life or death matter.

What about your savings account? That money could be in a money market fund, but you haven’t bothered to move it. How much in net interest income is made because of that friction?

The coming years will be some of the most interesting for investors who are intrigued by paradigm shifts and their ripple effects.

I, for one, could not be more excited to see how it all plays out and invest through the changes.

NEW Industry developments , Regulations is something one should never Ignore

IRDAI's draft proposes:
1) Nil commission on new-vehicle third-party motor, 5% cap on OD
2) Health capped at 15% first year, 5% on renewals
3) Tighter EoM limits, plus no mandatory bundling of insurance with loans
Motor commissions average ~24% today. Credit-linked insurance via NBFCs pays ~42% .

Start with PB Fintech & Turtlemint because they are purest play on this development . Health, term and motor are the core of Policybazaar's revenue, and potentially there could be commissions cut by a third to a half which could lead to substantial cut in earnings

Now look at the chart - Insurance income as % of PBT:
L&T Finance 25.6% | Poonawalla 17.8% | Chola 16.3% | Bajaj Finance 10.0% | Shriram 2.6%
Lose even half of it, and L&T Finance gives up ~13% of PBT.

Summing it up : It's a draft, comments are open till Oct 25, However even if the drafts doesnt materialise this could be a perception derating factor to entire space.

This is the power of tracking NEW developments , which one has to look during Anti thesis pointers as well.

Not a buy/sell recommendation. DYOR.

The global semiconductor chemicals market is valued at USD 51.5 bn in 2023 is expected to grow at a CAGR of 6% reaching USD 68.9bn by 2028.

The growth will be driven by the 5G rollout and rising demand for consumer electronics, IoT, and electric vehicles, all of which require high-purity chemicals for lithography and wafer manufacturing.

The global photoresist chemicals market valued at USD 2.3bn in 2023 is expected to reach USD 3.1bn by 2028 at a 5.5% CAGR.

Memory chip manufacturing consumes 10x higher material volumes compared to logic chips. While logic materials command higher per-unit pricing,
memory chips drive massive volume scale for chemical suppliers.

Accelerated adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is pushing CPU demand, which will directly pull up High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and DRAM chip requirements.

Demand for SEMICONDUCTOR chemicals and photoresist chemicals is going to increase going forward.

items.description_html:
Why ACE did a JV with KATO?

-ACE and Japan's Kato Works signed the definitive investment and shareholders agreement on 11 March 2026 and incorporated ACE KATO Private Limited, a 50:50 entity with total capital of 200crores with Kato putting in ₹100crores.

-With the base in Haryana and production of truck cranes, crawler cranes and rough terrain cranes for India and export markets. The plant is an 11-acre facility with roughly ₹200 crore of initial investment.

-ACE moved its existing Heavy Cranes Business i.e. ₹85.77 crore of FY25 standalone revenue, 2.58% of the total into the JV on a slump sale basis, with ACE subscribing to JV shares as consideration, taking its holding from 99% down to the 50:50 split, targeted for completion by 30 June 2026.

Why it's interesting:

-ACE's core is pick-and-carry, where it's the global volume leader but the segment is mature, cyclical and low-ticket. Truck, crawler and rough terrain cranes are the high-capacity end and the segment Indian OEMs have never cracked, where demand has been met largely by imported new and used machines from Chinese, Japanese and European names.

-The barrier there is engineering, not assembly: boom design, hydraulics, load-moment control, heavy structural fabrication. A JV buys that capability instead of spending a decade developing it.

The structure is also capital-efficient.

-ACE is risking roughly ₹100 crore of its own money and contributing a business that was 2.6% of revenue, for a call option on a segment with ticket sizes many multiples of pick-and-carry, and with end markets of refineries, metros, wind, ports, data centres, defence that are structurally growing.

-Kato's side of the logic is explicit: expanding overseas sales is a core plank of its three-year mid-term plan, and India gives it a cost base to export from

items.title: Consumers may eventually move to saying this to their person AI assistant: Find me running shoes under 8000, deliver them before Friday, use whichever...
items.description_html:
Consumers may eventually move to saying this to their person AI assistant: Find me running shoes under 8000, deliver them before Friday, use whichever website/app or a card gives me the best offer. You need agentic payment protocol built on UPI.

Conventionally, UPI has always required human to enter a PIN while AI is capable of find best deal. P3P by Pine Labs is designed to allow an authorised agent to complete the transaction without bringing the human back into every checkout.

Then, there is also UPI Reserve Pay.

A user can currently authorise up to 10000, after which multiple debits can occur against that reserved pool without repeated authorisation, subject to the mandate's limits.

And this becomes reality: You have 8000. Buy groceries for this week. Stay within my dietary requirements. Don't spend more than 2000 at any one merchant.

But the bigger story is not AI makes payments. Agentic commerce potentially changes merchant discovery itself.

An agent needs machine-readable access to:

- catalogue
- price
- inventory
- delivery
- offers
- refund rules
- credit/EMI
- payment methods
- merchant reputation

This reemphasizes thesis on build data products around agentic usecases.

Who else is doing what:

Razorpay already has an Agentic Payments Suite covering LLM checkout, in-app agents, voice commerce, UPI Reserve Pay and AI-ready APIs/MCP.

PayU is also enabling merchants to accept orders and payments from first- and third-party AI agents.

Visa and Mastercard are building the trust/tokenisation layer globally.

items.title: For an enterprise, self training open weight model is not the path of least resistance always. While open weight gives them freedom, it also adds over...
items.description_html:
For an enterprise, self training open weight model is not the path of least resistance always. While open weight gives them freedom, it also adds overhead elsewhere. And frontier labs are learning this smarlty enough. I see companies that drive enterprise with their ERPs adopting reasoning partners.

SAP: Anthropic, Claude
Microsoft Dynamics: OpenAI
Oracle: Cohere Command R+ & Meta Llama with native claude support

Frontier LLMs are selft-hosted, self-managed, giving enterprise much needed control, data protection levers & resource management. This is much better than hiring a whole team, maintaining open weight models for businesses that do not need complex reasoning needs that drug discovery, space research for e.g. needs.

This is a major trade off, and early signs point to direction that's away from open weight models.

items.title: RT Swapnil Srivastav: 🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame. Here’s ...
items.description_html:
RT Swapnil Srivastav
🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html: In my experience, this is probably the first time the Mid & Small cap indices have outperformed the Nifty 50 during a crisis time. It's also extremely rare to see the Mid & Small cap indices (avg of the two) beating the Nifty 50 near the bottom of the cycle. Their avg CAGR has outperformed during the last two tough years as well as all the below trailing years. I am not that surprised as their balance sheet, P&L and cash flow quality has substantially improved post COVID. I believe the biggest multi-baggers will emerge from this space as the earnings growth differential will be significant going forward. Because of the quality differential today vs during pre-COVID period, I would be surprised if their valuations correct to levels seen during the previous crashes. We probably have the best corporate quality and least stressed financials currently compared to any other previous big crisis.

items.description_html: Given that oil price is the biggest impact India and many other countries  are facing today because of the war, a coordinated effort to reduce fuel usage may help reduce major impact. During COVID the world went into a complete shut down and oil prices had dropped to below $20 and futures had crashed to -$37 in April 2020. items.title: As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/Mar...
items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight

items.title: The next global crisis may not be about oil, chips, or energy. It could simply be about WATER. The numbers are staggering: • 2.1 bn people still lack...
items.description_html:
The next global crisis may not be about oil, chips, or energy. It could simply be about WATER.

The numbers are staggering:

• 2.1 bn people still lack access to safe drinking water
• 3.4 bn lack safely managed sanitation
• 50%+ of global wastewater remains untreated
• Freshwater availability is declining 7% every decade
• Global water consumption is already 25% higher vs 2000

And this is increasingly an economic problem too.
Water scarcity already costs industries ~$80 bn annually, while nearly $70 trillion of global GDP could be at risk by 2050.

We often talk about energy security, semiconductor security and food security. Water security deserves a place in the same conversation.

Over the coming decades, treating, recycling, desalinating and using every litre of water more efficiently will move from being an environmental priority to an economic necessity.

Numbers Src: WABAG FY26 Annual Report

items.title: India’s next $500bn opportunity may simply be money moving from the bank account to the markets! Macquarie: India Capital Markets | A Powerful $500bn...
items.description_html:
India’s next $500bn opportunity may simply be money moving from the bank account to the markets!

Macquarie: India Capital Markets | A Powerful $500bn Flywheel

Macquarie says nearly 50% of India’s household financial savings still sit in cash & deposits — creating a powerful multi-year financialisation runway.

Its capital-markets pecking order: GROWW > MCX > BSE > NSE > Angel One, with opportunities across broking, exchanges, commodities and market infrastructure.

Key Points

* Nearly 50% of India’s financial household savings still remain in cash and deposits; we see a powerful multiyear growth backdrop for market infrastructure firms as capital shifts into financial assets.
* Regulation has strengthened trust, expanded participation, and increased resiliency in capital markets.
* Singapore, Thailand, and Malaysia are progressing through similar market-deepening catalysts to India, creating a long runway for capital market growth across the region.

We initiate coverage of India exchanges and brokers: Based on our multi-factor scoring and ranking, our pecking order is GROWW > MCX > BSE > NSE > ANGELONE.

* GROWW (OP; TP Rs260) is our preferred broker, supported by its customer-acquisition engine, cross-sell opportunity, margin-expansion runway and free-cash-flow potential.
* MCX (OP; TP Rs3,820) combines a strong commodity F&O franchise with a substantially under-penetrated asset class.
* BSE (OP; TP Rs4,000) offers an opportunity to participate in share gains in cash equities and F&O and non-transaction revenue growth.
* NSE (OP; TP Rs1,965) is the lynchpin for India's financialisation, with steady growth, margins and cash generation.
* ANGELONE (N; TP Rs285) has a recognised franchise but share losses and lower margin weaken the relative risk-reward

My view: We often focus on where the Nifty will be next year. The much bigger structural story is how Indians will save over the next decade. Even a gradual shift from deposits towards MFs, equities, ETFs, bonds and other financial assets can create a massive flywheel across the entire capital-market ecosystem.

Src: Macquarie | No reco

items.title: RT Madhav Chanchani: One of the wildest "what could have been" story for India’s venture capital industry.. That’s because back in 2009, three ventu...
items.description_html:
RT Madhav Chanchani
One of the wildest "what could have been" story for India’s venture capital industry..

That’s because back in 2009, three venture firms - Elevation Capital (then SAIF Partners), Tiger Global and Norwest Venture Partners - collectively held about 10% stake in NSE.

But when NSE lists on September 24 at Rs 4.42 lakh crore ($46 billion) valuation, these firms won’t be seen prominently on its cap table in what is India's second largest IPO.

The three firms had all picked up the stake at a valuation of around Rs 10,000-15,000 crore ($1-1.6 billion as per exchange rates now) for NSE.

This would have meant over 40 times returns by now, and an outcome collectively worth over Rs 40,000 crore or about $4.5 billion at the IPO.

While SAIF had picked up the largest stake (5%) in 2007, Tiger (3%) and Norwest (2%) picked up post financial crisis in 2009.

But then came the long wait for an IPO.

By late 2015 and early 2016, foreign investors sent formal notices to the NSE board saying that the management was "dragging its feet" on its listing. NSE management was resisting because law required it to cross-list on a rival exchange (like the BSE), exposing them to a competitor's regulation.

By December 2016, NSE filed for an IPO at Rs 45,000 crore valuation. But it was shelved after the co-location data-access scandal triggered years of SEBI show-cause notices and the governance saga around former CEO Chitra Ramkrishna. The plans for listing stayed frozen.

Rather than wait it out, most of these investors started selling down gradually from 2018-19 given the typical venture fund life is 10-12 years.

By 2023, they sold off their shares in tranches, when the peak grey-market valuation for NSE was roughly Rs 1.9 lakh crore ($20 billion).

This would mean that they would have made about 8x to 16x returns for all these investors - which are still good returns.

But not close to over 40x they would have made through the IPO if they still held stake, given the valuation surge over the last few years.

Tiger Global is the exception among the three, as it still holds 0.64% stake after partially exiting most of its holding over the years. It is not selling in the IPO.

This unsold stake is worth Rs 2,830 crore ($300 million) at the IPO price.

items.title: RT The Khel India: 🚨 INDIA eFOOTBALL GOT ROBBED AT THE ASIAN GAMES, 2026! 💔🎮 India’s Danial Patel & Chinmay Sahoo were eliminated from the A...
items.description_html:
RT The Khel India
🚨 INDIA eFOOTBALL GOT ROBBED AT THE ASIAN GAMES, 2026! 💔🎮

India’s Danial Patel & Chinmay Sahoo were eliminated from the Asian Games after a bizarre turn of events in the Group F.

India had drawn 0-0 against Uzbekistan in their opening match. Uzbekistan then defeated Mongolia heavily, winning 6-3 and 12-0 across the mobile and console games.

India then faced Mongolia, but the match never took place.

Mongolia’s team leader arrived just 3 minutes after the required check-in time. Under the tournament rules, India were awarded a 0-0 forfeit win.

The problem? A 0-0 win gave India the victory and points, but no goal-difference advantage.

India protested and requested officials to allow the match to be played, but the request was rejected. They were also told they could pay $500 for a judge panel review, but the Indian team decided not to pursue it.

As a result, India finished with one win and one draw, but their goal difference remained 0. Uzbekistan topped the group on goal difference.

India also missed out on qualification as one of the best second-placed teams, with Thailand (+3) and Saudi Arabia (+2) taking those spots.

A frustrating end for India, especially with Danial Patel being the reigning Asian eFootball champion.

[ The Bridge ]

Will plough through Shruti's piece slowly. I've always thought existing liability laws suffice (in countries with state capacity) but the autonomy question is interesting.

Organized players can ensure KYC, credit card linked billing, some liability risk insurance etc. so OpenAI, astra, Google etc can ensure KYC for token usage etc.

Or we wonder about building a second life as the years slip by.

Is it doable? Yes!

items.description_html:
Macquarie on India Insurance: IRDAI has released its long-awaited consultation paper on commission regulations.

@CNBCTV18Live

Stocks in focus:
PB Fintech: Most exposed given earnings sensitivity to take rates; ~2ppt compression could erode EBITDA by ~25%, all else equal.
SBI & SBI Life: Relatively insulated as SBI charges lower commissions; LIC benefits from higher agent limits across product categories.
Private banks: Axis & HDFC Bank more exposed than ICICI & Kotak, given higher contribution of insurance fee income to revenue/PBT.
NBFCs: Corporate agents such as L&T Finance vulnerable, given credit-life policies’ sizeable contribution to fee income.

They cap insurance commissions as a percentage, spread the payouts across the policy terms, and reduce larger distributor strangleholders. Also promotes direct investment by customers.

RT Sina Toossi
Significant comments today amid UNGA U.S.-Iran diplomacy from Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s top national security body, the Supreme National Security Council.

He says Pezeshkian & Araghchi went to New York to convey Iran’s internally agreed terms, not negotiate new ones: “There has been no discussion of changing the conditions.” Araghchi was tasked with transmitting them through mediators.

Rezaei says Iran won’t return to the diplomacy of the Islamabad ceasefire. He says Washington must first accept Iran’s conditions and has “4–5 days” to act.

The short deadline amounts to an implicit threat of further escalation if it doesn’t.

He also warned neighboring states aiding US pressure on Iranian aviation: block Iranian flights and “your airports will have no flights.”

His message overall is that Tehran is open to diplomacy, but its terms are fixed and US action must come first.

items.title: ORACLE'S DATACENTER 'FORCE MAJEURE' Impact here: Oracle -> Bloom -> MTAR Tech Oracle was -4% & Bloom was -3%. What has happened -> Oracle sent a “for...
items.description_html:
ORACLE'S DATACENTER 'FORCE MAJEURE'

Impact here: Oracle -> Bloom -> MTAR Tech

Oracle was -4% & Bloom was -3%.

What has happened -> Oracle sent a “force majeure” notice to the builders of its Project Jupiter future datacenter in New Mexico.

Project Jupiter is a 4-building campus in New Mexico - roughly 1,400 acres outside El Paso. OpenAI is the primary Oracle customer for the site. Power was expected to be delivered via Bloom Energy fuel cells which would be fueled with natural gas.

The Green Chile Project pipeline - a 17-mile gas pipeline being built by Energy Transfer to supply the site - has been delayed from August 2026 to February 2027.

The delay follows repeated refusals by the New Mexico State Land Office to grant right-of-way permits across state-owned trust land. Local officials & environmental groups have opposed the project, citing concerns about climate impact and use of natural resources.

Bloom needs that gas supply in order to start commissioning at the site.

The 2.5 GW associated with Project Jupiter is the largest deployment in Bloom’s disclosed pipeline against its backlog.

RT Nithin Kamath
I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today's IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is a good reminder.

Broking is no different. A change in rules around retail F&O trading, how brokers can earn on client float, MTF requirements, or any of several other areas can change the economics of the business almost overnight.

So when valuing regulated businesses, you can't just extrapolate current revenues and profits into the future. One regulation change can alter the economics, and the stock price along with it.

Pretty much everything in fintech comes with this risk 😬

items.title: RT Dario Amodei: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its ...
items.description_html:
RT Dario Amodei
Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend.

The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans).

More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains.

In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries.

Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology.

I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out.

items.title: RT ValueEquity: Neuland Labs notes from recent plant visit by @ekta_batra , sharing my notes : 1) Journey for peptides started when we were trying to ...
items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
Neuland Labs notes from recent plant visit by @ekta_batra , sharing my notes :

1) Journey for peptides started when we were trying to build partnerships with innovators, back then peptides were not that well known
2) 7000L capacity in module 1 , clinical pipeline of 8-9 in phase 2/3 ,all in peptides , once we had the funnel we started working on this
3) Peptide API manufacturing for Innovators is $9B , no peptides for innovators are being made in India , most are made for generic players
4) 2 projects are going to occupy most of module 1 , they are going to get commercialised , general outlook on asset turns , module 1 20M$ investment , 1.5 times asset turns , as these 2 are in the end of phase 3 and heading to commercial as innovators validate the phase 3
4) China /EU is the competition , we are having the process design edge , bespoke CDM0 , we have that niche ability to start from small batches , to large batches , small molecule edge from LPPS( Liquid phase peptide synthesis ) and module 1 is Solid Phase peptide synthesis , a mix of both is ideal , and what we bring to the table
5) We will not be making commercial peptides for GLP-1 , we have something in weight loss ( 2) some of them are in metabolic and neurological
6) Cross next gen peptides are what we are focusing on beyond peptides , there are more than 1000 peptides in the trials now
7) Oncology is important for peptides ,Module 1 is veyr suited for Onco API's , that would be what we would be pursuing with
8) Aspirationally in India peptides should be multi billion dollar opp for India , cycle times are longer
9)Nature of business is Lumpy until we break out of the few molecules sizing , as shipments are based very lumpy in small molecules as these are campaign linked ( CMS)
10) GDS , 15% , steady state guidance , 15-20% annual is reasonable growth wise , as we are conservative
11) Vision is to make Neuland to be an essential partner , multiple modalities , partner of choice , and focusing on development and manucturing
12) We are looking at capabilty based M&A in the US not capacity based , we feel the need to be closer to the customer
13) China +1 is real , as innovators are keen to look at India and EU , several projects are moving out of China , RFP we got in the last 3M are the highs

Loving this plant visit series and a lot to learn and understand , thanks @ekta_batra and team , link for full video :

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pRPw0RVXxRs&list=LL&index=3

items.title: Bansal Wiring, business worth reading : Largest Stainless Steel Wire manufacturers in India by volume 3,000+ SKUs – highest among all steel wire manu...
items.description_html:
Bansal Wiring, business worth reading : Largest Stainless Steel Wire manufacturers in India by volume 3,000+ SKUs – highest among all steel wire manufacturers in India 5,000+ Customers across various industries and FY26 capacity utilization: management stated ~67–68%. This year expecting 400 crores of Cash Flow, ROCE improvement to 25% targets in the next few years ( currently 15% )

1st quarter F27, specialty wire we are getting trial orders at better margins, post 4 stage validations we have 2 lakh tonnes target, this will be trajectory changing product for the company , no customer concentration , no industry/customer is major risk to the company , we are also seeing the demand trend stabilising , expecting Q1 to be weaker on margins ( cost + Lag 35 days ) , and 3 quarters ahead will be 20% growth , focusing on cash generation aggressively for incremental growth , this cash to growth capex loop is what they are trying to master

Constantly focusing on market share gains, we have lot of experience in the ecosystem that gives us a lot of confidence to grow Specialty wires currently <3–4% with expectation to start forming part of mix going forward , which is a classic value added product thesis for better margins that involve incremental volumes on realisations being better hence changing the mix positively , weak Q1 is consensus expectation is here pretty much , growth is second half of the year

Bansal Wires , took a weak Q1 by choice
1) Did not pass price hike to customers as they have been with them for a long time
2) took a hit from INR 7 a kg blended and we came down to INR 2 a kg, wherein we absorbed all that cost. Now once we had that cost increase, the new orders that we booked were again with the right prices.
3) Classic Mix play as specialty picks up with better realisations
4) FY27 operating cash flow target of ₹400 crore.

Will be an interesting company , question is can they replicate an APL apollo tubes in a steel wires commodity segment , time will tell..

items.title: Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue gre...
items.description_html:
Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting

Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue grew at ~55% CAGR between FY24 and FY26, while EBITDA margin expanded to ~14%, RoCE stood at ~26% and RoE at ~35%. Despite the sharp scale-up, debtor days remain relatively controlled versus several listed EPC peers.

The key monitor remains cash-flow conversion, as strong historical growth has resulted in higher receivables, retention money and working-capital requirements. However, this needs to be seen alongside the expansion in execution: the order book increased from ~₹684 crore in March 2026 to ₹916.6 crore by July 2026, while of which majority is funded bybnodal agencies like World Bank, providing relatively stronger payment visibility. The company also highlights that projects are largely supported by Central schemes and institutional financiers such as PFC, REC, ADB and the World Bank.

Importantly, Swastika is gradually moving from conventional power-distribution EPC toward more specialised and higher-value segments. It entered power transmission and renewable-energy infrastructure in 2026, while larger project credentials are expected to improve its eligibility for ₹900+ crore tenders, where management indicates competition is relatively lower. This can potentially improve both the quality and scale of the opportunity set over time.

At the IPO price band of ₹175–185, the company is valued at roughly ₹597–631 crore post-issue market capitalisation, translating to approximately 14.4x–15.2x FY26 earnings and ~1.2x FY26 revenue, based on the FY26 PAT of ₹41.4 crore. Against its historical growth, return ratios, funded order-book visibility and transition toward higher-value EPC projects, the valuation appears reasonable, with execution and working-capital conversion remaining the key factors to track.

items.description_html:
A-One Steels ~ Building A Cost-Efficient, Integrated Green Steel Platform

A-One Steels is transitioning from a regional TMT manufacturer into a more integrated steel player, focusing on backward integration, capacity expansion, product diversification and wider market reach.

Integrated Steel Value Chain: The company operates across the entire value chain — sponge iron → billets → coils → pipes/tubes → TMT, along with ferro alloys and met coke, enabling better control over raw materials and production costs.

Capacity Expansion Driving Scale: MS billet capacity has increased from 4.55 lakh MTPA in FY24 to 5.70 lakh MTPA in FY26, alongside expansion in TMT and MS pipe capacities.

Strengthening Raw Material Security: Upcoming initiatives include a 6 lakh MTPA iron ore beneficiation plant, manganese ore mining lease and a 10 MW waste heat recovery power plant to improve cost competitiveness.

New Product Opportunities: The Koppal facility provides scope to expand into products such as pellets, alloy billets and crash barriers, increasing the addressable market.

Green Energy Advantage: Around 83.2% of energy consumption is sourced from green energy, supporting lower operating costs and improving sustainability credentials.

FY26 Profitability Recovery: The company reported Rs. 4,167 Cr revenue, Rs. 304 Cr EBITDA and Rs. 127 Cr PAT in FY26, compared with EBITDA of Rs. 174 Cr and PAT of Rs. 8 Cr in FY25.

Efficient Asset Utilisation: Net fixed asset turnover stood at 6.93x in FY26, indicating strong utilisation of existing manufacturing assets.

Brand-Led Expansion: The company is strengthening its A-One Gold brand while expanding distribution reach across retail and institutional customers.

Acquisition-Led Growth Strategy: A-One Steels has historically scaled through acquisitions and continues to evaluate underutilised assets to accelerate capacity growth.

Export Readiness: CBAM compliance initiatives are underway to access European markets and tap demand for lower-carbon steel.

The Bigger Transition:
Regional Steel Manufacturer → Integrated Steel Producer → Diversified Product Platform → Pan-India & Export-Oriented Player
Key monitorables remain capacity ramp-up, leverage management (1.17x gross debt/equity), execution of backward integration projects and sustainability of FY26 profitability improvement.

items.title: Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather t...
items.description_html:
Ashutosh Fibre IPO : A Technical Yarn Player Moving Towards Higher-Value Products

Ashutosh Fibre is an interesting play on technical textiles rather than conventional textile demand. The company manufactures specialised yarns engineered for specific performance characteristics such as high tensile strength, flame resistance, heat resistance, chemical stability, abrasion resistance and anti-static properties.

Its products ultimately find applications across defence, protective clothing, automotive components, filtration and pollution control, geotextiles, industrial fabrics, thermal insulation, packaging and home furnishing.

Why the Business Looks Interesting

1. The biggest change is happening in the revenue mix and profitability.

Revenue from operations increased only modestly from Rs. 109.9 crore in FY24 to Rs. 117.4 crore in FY26, but EBITDA increased from Rs. 16.1 crore to Rs. 31.1 crore over the same period.

As a result:

EBITDA margin: 14.7% → 15.6% → 26.5%
PAT: Rs. 7.0 crore → Rs. 8.5 crore → Rs. 16.0 crore
PAT margin: 6.4% → 7.5% → 13.7%
ROCE: 21.0% → 16.3% → 26.3%

So FY26 growth was less about topline acceleration and more about a sharp improvement in business mix and profitability.

The most interesting development is the shift away from Indutech towards higher-growth categories.

2. What Industries Does It Serve?

Its yarn portfolio gives it exposure to several specialised applications:

Protech: Flame-retardant and heat-resistant yarns used in PPE, safety apparel and industrial thermal barriers.

Mobiltech: Friction-resistant yarns used in brake pads, clutch facings and transmission components.

Indutech: Filtration, filter cartridges, ropes, webbings and other industrial applications.

Hometech: Home furnishing textiles, carpets and filtration media.

Its broader product range includes para-aramid-based spun yarn, high-tenacity polyester, meta-aramid, FR viscose, modacrylic yarn, polypropylene yarn, stainless-steel yarn and specialised friction-spun yarns.
That creates exposure to structural themes including industrial safety, defence, automotive, pollution control and filtration, infrastructure and specialised manufacturing.

3. Capacity Is Becoming The Next Constraint

The company's main technical/synthetic yarn capacity stood at 3,750 MT in FY26, while production reached 3,619 MT.

That means utilisation has increased sharply:

FY24: 80.2%
FY25: 86.6%
FY26: 96.5%

This is important because the existing facility is approaching full utilisation precisely when newer categories such as Protech are scaling.

Ashutosh Fibre therefore plans to expand within its existing Petlad, Gujarat facility, adding compact spinning systems and high-value yarn attachments such as the Pinter Hard Core system.

Expanding within the existing facility should allow the company to leverage existing infrastructure, workforce and administrative resources — potentially making the expansion more capital-efficient.
Moving Downstream Into Modacrylic Fabrics
Another interesting strategy is forward integration.

4. Moving up in Value Chain
Ashutosh already manufactures modacrylic-based yarn used for high-performance fabrics. It now wants to move into manufacturing and selling the fabric itself.

The company has started trial production through third-party weaving and processing facilities and is targeting approximately 20,000 metres of modacrylic-based fabric sales per month.

The important part is that Ashutosh's own yarn would be consumed as the raw material.

This potentially allows it to move from being only a yarn supplier towards a higher-value finished technical textile product, improving value addition and potentially margins.

5. Exports Could Become Another Growth Lever

Exports are already meaningful:

FY24: Rs. 47.9 crore — 43.6% of revenue
FY25: Rs. 43.4 crore — 38.1%
FY26: Rs. 45.8 crore — 39.0%

The company plans to use additional capacity to target new international markets for specialised technical yarns.

Ashutosh Fibre is interesting because three transitions are happening simultaneously:

Volume → Value: Higher-value technical and performance yarns are becoming more important.

Yarn → Fabric: The company is attempting to move downstream into modacrylic technical fabrics.

Domestic + Existing Exports → Larger Global Opportunity: Nearly 40% of revenue already comes from exports, while new capacity is intended partly to deepen international penetration.

IPO coming at 12.5 PE

items.title: Regulatory risk is real & must never be ignored while investing We have seen this across multiple sectors: - IRDAI : commission caps, expense limits a...
items.description_html:
Regulatory risk is real & must never be ignored while investing

We have seen this across multiple sectors:

- IRDAI : commission caps, expense limits and distribution rules can directly impact insurers

- RBI : lending rules, risk weights, provisioning norms, digital lending guidelines etc

- SEBI : changes in F&O regulations, exchange frameworks, other regulations etc

- Income Tax & GST : tax demands, retrospective interpretations, compliance disputes etc

- US FDA : observations, warning letters or import alerts

- TRAI / DoT - tariff rules, spectrum norms, telecom regulations

- Environment authorities : approvals, pollution norms & plant shutdown risks for manufacturing companies

- DGCA : regulatory changes for airlines & aviation companies

- Government policy : duties, subsidies, import restrictions, export bans, PLI related changes etc

There have also been episodes around hospital pricing regulations, gold import duty changes, windfall taxes, gaming GST changes & several others.

We have seen several such examples over the years - Delta Corp, IIFL Finance, IEX and many others getting impacted because of regulatory or policy changes.

This is why diversification matters!

items.title: RT Dhirendra Kumar: A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give invest...
items.description_html:
RT Dhirendra Kumar
A few weeks ago I wrote that a tool every investor can buy cannot set any investor apart. Why AI investing tools don't give investors an edge: https://vro.in/s229348. The line came from Vineet Nayar's new book, Humans First, Machines Second. His point is plain. AI is powerful and everyone has it. Something everyone has cannot make anyone special.
That left a question I did not answer. If the machine is common, what is uncommon?
I think the machine has taken the middle of the work and left us the two ends. It has not taken the beginning, which is deciding what question to ask. It has not taken the end, which is deciding whether the answer is any good.
Ask an AI to analyse a fund and you will get a competent analysis of that fund. It will not tell you that the reader's real problem is not this fund but whether he should be in this category at all. Knowing that comes from thirty years of reading letters from investors.
The machine will also give you ten sensible options. Picking the one that suits this reader in this market is not calculation. It is judgement, and judgement is mostly the memory of having been wrong before.
Then there is the story. The investor who sold everything in March 2020 did not lack information. He lacked a story strong enough to hold him when the fear came. Nobody gets that story from a prompt. AI can help you invent. It cannot invent.
One more thing. The machine agrees with you. Tell it you like a stock and it will find reasons to like it. What a person needs from an advisor or an editor is the opposite: someone willing to say no.
Nayar says the danger is not smarter machines but people losing faith in what only they can do. In our business, that is the risk worth worrying about.

items.title: RT Nithin Kamath: I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today's IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is...
items.description_html:
RT Nithin Kamath
I keep saying this: for any regulated business, the biggest risk is regulatory risk. Today's IRDAI draft on insurance commissions is a good reminder.

Broking is no different. A change in rules around retail F&O trading, how brokers can earn on client float, MTF requirements, or any of several other areas can change the economics of the business almost overnight.

So when valuing regulated businesses, you can't just extrapolate current revenues and profits into the future. One regulation change can alter the economics, and the stock price along with it.

Pretty much everything in fintech comes with this risk 😬

At that time Indian refiners who benefitted massively were RIL, MRPL AND CPCL

RIL — the big direct winner. Most of what it makes is transport fuel, and the SEZ refinery is built to export.

To put that number in perspective, if Muthoot were ranked alongside countries by central bank gold reserves, it would sit at roughly 25th globally.

Singapore: ~200 tonnes
Muthoot Finance: ~200 tonnes
Brazil: ~175 tonnes

Of course, Muthoot doesn’t own this gold—it is pledged by borrowers. But the sheer scale of the collateral sitting in its vaults is remarkable.

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.title: India’s hydro is empty. Australia’s mines are dry. One weather event, two very different commodity outcomes. Super El Niño is at +2.51°C and still...
items.description_html:
India’s hydro is empty. Australia’s mines are dry. One weather event, two very different commodity outcomes.

Super El Niño is at +2.51°C and still climbing toward +3°C.

The 15-second take

Thermal coal: bullish

Iron ore + met coal: mildly bearish

Thermal coal

India’s weakest monsoon in 17 years (–15% rain). Reservoirs at 5-year lows. Less hydro = more coal burn. Indonesia barging also gets squeezed. Demand shock + modest supply hit.

Iron ore

Drier Australia = higher mine output + fewer cyclones (normally knocks ~10% off Q1 exports). Brazil net mildly positive for Vale. Simandou already ramping. Tape already soft (~$97, FOB near 18-month lows). Extra reliable tonnes = pressure, not a crash.

Met coal
Same story as iron ore: Queensland and Canada get easier operating conditions.

Weather is a tilt, not the whole tape. China steel and high-cost supply still run the show. But the split is clear: coal wants the drought, iron ore just got more tonnes.

items.title: RT Aditi Shrivastava: As 10-minute delivery & large product assortments become standard in quick commerce, platforms are running out of ways to tie in...
items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
As 10-minute delivery & large product assortments become standard in quick commerce, platforms are running out of ways to tie in users.

Swiggy is betting that what Instamart sells can provide the difference, driving customers to choose it over six rival apps.

Under a strategy called Switch, Swiggy Instamart is adding its own brands and exclusive products co-created with other companies. These products are marketed as higher-quality or better-for-you items.

This is not the usual private-label model built around lower prices. For example, two Swiggy-owned brands, Noice and Nectr, sit slightly above the mass market and sell on quality. The company believes customers will pay a little extra if the product feels sufficiently premium.

Private labels have already become a key part of Instamart. Around the time of Swiggy’s IPO in 2024, analysts and company insiders estimated that they accounted for 4-5% of gross order value.

That share has since increased to 8-9%, said people familiar with the business. Instamart’s GOV, meanwhile, grew from Rs 8,069 crore in FY24 to Rs 28,496 crore in FY26.

items.title: RT Nikesh Arora: This will be a bigger battle than anyone anticipates. It is only a matter of time before there is an Apple and Google version of Muse...
items.description_html:
RT Nikesh Arora
This will be a bigger battle than anyone anticipates. It is only a matter of time before there is an Apple and Google version of Muse and possibly TikTok, in addition to the frontier LLM agents. Maybe a commerce agent from Amazon.

Every app that is a services, marketplace or commerce app will need to existentially decide to open APIs for consumer agents to interact. Smaller players have no choice. Ad revenues are more than transaction fees, either the consumer benefits or distribution aggregators will demand a higher transaction fare.

I know I don't want an agent for each app. I would like my agent to be able to do tasks I require. We can already see consumers getting trained on that behavior by the frontier labs.

Those with network moats - restaurants, groceries, drivers might be able to withstand for a while, over time convenience and end user experience will win and they will have to align. Content moats (protected by copyright) could decide to allow agents or chose to hold on to the consumer interaction. I suspect other than the feeling of a lack of control, it won't change their economics.

Commoditized back ends will need to worry, insurance, tickets, hotels, services - if they don't adapt new players will.

items.title: One of the wildest "what could have been" story for India’s venture capital industry.. That’s because back in 2009, three venture firms - Elevation ...
items.description_html:
One of the wildest "what could have been" story for India’s venture capital industry..

That’s because back in 2009, three venture firms - Elevation Capital (then SAIF Partners), Tiger Global and Norwest Venture Partners - collectively held about 10% stake in NSE.

But when NSE lists on September 24 at Rs 4.42 lakh crore ($46 billion) valuation, these firms won’t be seen prominently on its cap table in what is India's second largest IPO.

The three firms had all picked up the stake at a valuation of around Rs 10,000-15,000 crore ($1-1.6 billion as per exchange rates now) for NSE.

This would have meant over 40 times returns by now, and an outcome collectively worth over Rs 40,000 crore or about $4.5 billion at the IPO.

While SAIF had picked up the largest stake (5%) in 2007, Tiger (3%) and Norwest (2%) picked up post financial crisis in 2009.

But then came the long wait for an IPO.

By late 2015 and early 2016, foreign investors sent formal notices to the NSE board saying that the management was "dragging its feet" on its listing. NSE management was resisting because law required it to cross-list on a rival exchange (like the BSE), exposing them to a competitor's regulation.

By December 2016, NSE filed for an IPO at Rs 45,000 crore valuation. But it was shelved after the co-location data-access scandal triggered years of SEBI show-cause notices and the governance saga around former CEO Chitra Ramkrishna. The plans for listing stayed frozen.

Rather than wait it out, most of these investors started selling down gradually from 2018-19 given the typical venture fund life is 10-12 years.

By 2023, they sold off their shares in tranches, when the peak grey-market valuation for NSE was roughly Rs 1.9 lakh crore ($20 billion).

This would mean that they would have made about 8x to 16x returns for all these investors - which are still good returns.

But not close to over 40x they would have made through the IPO if they still held stake, given the valuation surge over the last few years.

Tiger Global is the exception among the three, as it still holds 0.64% stake after partially exiting most of its holding over the years. It is not selling in the IPO.

This unsold stake is worth Rs 2,830 crore ($300 million) at the IPO price.
